Euclid. Around three hundred BCE, an ancient Greek mathematician who compiled and systematised geometry into The Elements, the most influential mathematical text in history. Working in Alexandria during the Ptolemaic dynasty, he distilled the geometric knowledge accumulated by centuries of Greek mathematicians into a carefully ordered hierarchy of axioms, definitions, and propositions. He established a deductive framework that remained the gold standard for rigorous proof for two thousand years. His work shaped not only mathematics but philosophy, education, and the very meaning of logical certainty.

The Elements contains thirteen books, covering plane and solid geometry, number theory, and the theory of ratios. Each book builds carefully from axioms—self-evident truths—precise definitions of key terms, and geometric postulates that seem obviously true. Theorems follow by deductive proof from these foundations. The five postulates of Euclidean geometry include the controversial parallel postulate: through a point not on a line, exactly one parallel line can be drawn. This postulate differs from the others in that it is less obviously self-evident.

The Pythagorean theorem is proven in Book I as Proposition forty-seven, with the converse also appearing. Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes using a clever proof by contradiction—if you add one to the product of all known primes, the resulting number cannot be divisible by any of them, so it must be prime or have a prime factor not in the original list. His construction of the Platonic solids, the five regular polyhedra—tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron—appears in Book XIII.

Euclid's geometry is entirely constructive, showing how to build figures using compass and straightedge, with no coordinates needed. The greatest common divisor algorithm, the Euclidean algorithm, is essentially his method for reducing fractions to their simplest forms by repeated subtraction.

The parallel postulate haunted mathematicians for centuries. Every attempt to prove it from the other four postulates failed, eventually leading nineteenth-century mathematicians to ask a revolutionary question: what if the parallel postulate is false? The answer opened non-Euclidean geometry—hyperbolic and elliptic spaces—and revolutionised our understanding of space itself. For most of history, geometry meant Euclid, and his name was synonymous with mathematical proof. His Elements was the primary geometry textbook for two thousand years and remains a model of rigorous exposition.
